source_text:
3 μτ 21, 28–32 Τοῦτο βούλεται εἰπεῖν ἡ παραβολή, ὅτι οἱ μὲν τελῶναι καὶ αἱ
πόρναι μετανοήσαντες καὶ τὰ ἀρεστὰ τῷ θεῷ ποιήσαντες δικαιοῦνται Ἰωάννῃ
πεισθέντες, εἰ καὶ κατ' ἀρχὰς ἠπείθουν τῷ νόμῳ, μᾶλλον δὲ τῷ θεῷ.
thought_title: The parable's point: repentant tax collectors and prostitutes are justified
orientation: Theophilus is explaining the point of the parable of the two sons from Matthew 21:28–32, now stating what the parable means for the first group.
pass_a_gloss: This the parable wants to say: that the tax collectors and the prostitutes, having repented and having done the things pleasing to God, are justified, having been persuaded by John, even if at first they were disobeying the law, but rather God.

choices.why: Keeps the dative τῷ θεῷ as the one to whom the things are pleasing, matching the Greek construction.
Uses the fixed glossary rendering for this key theological term.
Keeps the dative of agent with the passive participle, showing John as the one who persuaded them.
Preserves the corrective force of μᾶλλον δὲ, which intensifies the disobedience from law to God himself.

bible_refs.note: The heading cites the parable of the two sons, which this passage interprets.

pass_b_english: This is what the parable wants to say: the tax collectors and the prostitutes repented and did the things pleasing to God, and so they are justified, having been persuaded by John—even though at first they were disobeying the law, or rather, disobeying God himself.

problems.quote: This is what the parable wants to say
problems.why: Unclear if author speaks or paraphrases another authority; no section attribution.
problems.fix: Clarify this is the patristic author's interpretation.

problems.quote: the first son is the Gentiles
problems.why: The 'first son' is the Gentiles who refused but later went; section u01-rem-early says 'the first son had refused' as if moving to a new actor, confusing the reader.
problems.fix: Clarify that the first son (Gentiles) initially refused but later repented and went.
